newsitem.title: HAITI: Criticized Disney contractor shuns Haiti.
newsitem.headline: Criticized Disney contractor shuns Haiti.

text.p: After scathing criticism of its work practices by international activists, Walt Disney Co.'s largest subcontractor in Haiti said Thursday it was slashing its business with local factories, leaving as many as 2,300 people jobless.
"Very little work will be contracted out to Haitian factories in the near term," said Cindy Knoebel, a spokesman for VF Corp., the parent company of Disney subcontractor H.H. Cutler.

Assembly workers sewing Disney-licensed clothing account for about 10 percent of the assembly industry in the impoverished Caribbean nation, which suffers from an 80 percent unemployment rate. Wages are as low as 28 cents an hour.

Citing those wages, and alleging that workers in Disney factories are treated poorly, activist groups have staged repeated protests in the United States and Europe against the entertainment giant and its contractors.

Pickets taunted high-paid Disney executives at the company's annual meeting, comparing their pay to the Haitian wages. Others have marched in New York and London, calling for boycotts and waging a high-profile "Mickey is a Rat" campaign over treatment of Haitian workers.
But given small likelihood of finding more work in the Western Hemisphere's poorest nation, the workers themselves expressed mixed emotions about the loss of their jobs.

"If I lose my job, I might die, but I'm half-dead already," said a worker waiting for a bus on a dusty street outside a factory in the capital this week. "I pay for the bus to come here, food and a juice, and when I get home I have barely anything left," she said, declining to give her name.
VF's Knoebel denied the pullout was due to bad publicity. She cited slumping sales of Disney children's clothing, which the Haitian factories specialise in, as the cause.
Nightgowns, caps and other products bearing characters from recent animated Disney movies have not sold as well as those tied to earlier films.
"From our point of view 'Lion King' was the peak," she said, referring to the company's smash kiddie film. "Disney has had other successes, but not at that level.

Charles Kernaghan, a founder of the "Mickey is a Rat" campaign at New York's National Labour Committee, said Cutler is leaving Haiti because it wants to use factories in China and Indonesia, where workers make as little as 6 cents per hour.
"Simply stated, H.H. Cutler is going after cheaper labour," he said, alleging that the company's sales are not slumping as it has claimed.

Officials at H.H. Cutler factories said no one was available in Haiti to comment. But a factory manager at L.V. Myles, a company that it not a Cutler subcontractor but also assembles Disney clothing, said demand and publicity could both have played a part.
"There certainly is a slump in demand. We're all feeling it," he said. "H.H. Cutler's decision to leave Haiti is likely due to a combination of both the drop in sales and bad publicity."
Critics blamed labour advocates outside of Haiti for co-opting the nation's cause and putting thousands of badly needed jobs at risk.
Kernaghan responded that both he and the workers were aware of the risks of protesting.

"We didn't do a single thing that wasn't consulted with Haitian workers on the ground," he said. "People told us it was a starvation wage, period. They asked us to take that and their demands to rights to better conditions and rights to organise to Disney."
Factory workers said they would not blame the foreign activists if they lose their jobs.

"They are fighting for a better life for us," said a woman who would only speak to a reporter around the corner from the factory. "Maybe they exploited us to make a point, but the company is exploiting us to make money."
